\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{さとう} (satou)}{さとう (satou)}]{\ja{さとう} (satou) — sugar}

\label{lesson:JA-C35-satou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for tofu, then the Japanese for salt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{さとう}}
\textbf{\ja{さとう}} — \emph{satou} — \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{さとう}} (\emph{satou}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{sa}, \textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{srae}) and \emph{tō}, \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{} (\emph{dang}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{うどん} (udon)}{うどん (udon)}]{\ja{うどん} (udon) — udon noodles}

\label{lesson:JA-C35-udon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for salt, then the Japanese for sugar.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{うどん}}
\textbf{\ja{うどん}} — \emph{udon} — \textquotedblleft{}udon noodles\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{うどん}} (\emph{udon}) is usually traced to a Chinese name for a kind of dumpling, written with two characters that JMdict also gives; the route and the change of meaning are not settled. JMdict marks it as usually written in kana.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{すし} (sushi)}{すし (sushi)}]{\ja{すし} (sushi) — sushi}

\label{lesson:JA-C35-sushi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for sugar, then the Japanese for udon noodles.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{すし}}
\textbf{\ja{すし}} — \emph{sushi} — \textquotedblleft{}sushi\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{すし}} (\emph{sushi}) is a native word, inherited rather than borrowed. The usual account derives it from an old adjective \emph{sushi}, \textquotedblleft{}sour\textquotedblright{}, for the vinegared rice. JMdict marks its common spelling with characters for \textquotedblleft{}long life\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}manage\textquotedblright{} as ateji, chosen for their sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{あさごはん} (asagohan)}{あさごはん (asagohan)}]{\ja{あさごはん} (asagohan) — breakfast}

\label{lesson:JA-C35-asagohan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for udon noodles, then the Japanese for sushi.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あさごはん}}
\textbf{\ja{あさごはん}} — \emph{asagohan} — \textquotedblleft{}breakfast\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あさごはん}} (\emph{asagohan}) mixes the two layers: native \emph{asa}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}, read as a kun'yomi, and \emph{gohan}, \textquotedblleft{}rice; a meal\textquotedblright{}, Sino-Japanese \emph{go}, \textquotedblleft{}honourable\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{han}, \textquotedblleft{}cooked rice\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{bjonX}), borrowed from Chinese (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{おかし} (okashi)}{おかし (okashi)}]{\ja{おかし} (okashi) — sweets, snacks}

\label{lesson:JA-C35-okashi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for sushi, then the Japanese for breakfast.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{おかし}}
\textbf{\ja{おかし}} — \emph{okashi} — \textquotedblleft{}sweets, snacks\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{おかし}} (\emph{okashi}) is the native polite prefix \emph{o-} with \emph{kashi}, \textquotedblleft{}sweets\textquotedblright{}, Sino-Japanese: \emph{ka}, \textquotedblleft{}fruit; cake\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{kwaX}), and \emph{shi}, a noun ending written with the character for \textquotedblleft{}child\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{tsiX}), borrowed from Chinese (JMdict; Unihan).
\end{cousinweb}
